content: Urinary incontinence affects a significant proportion of individuals following a stroke, with 40% to 60% experiencing it during hospitalization, 25% still affected at discharge, and 15% remaining incontinent one year post-stroke. This review aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of various interventions for managing urinary incontinence in adults at least one month after a stroke. Behavioral Interventions Evidence of low quality suggests that behavioral interventions may reduce the average number of incontinent episodes within a 24-hour period. However, the reduction was not statistically significant (mean difference [MD] –1.00, 95% confidence interval [CI] –2.74 to 0.74; 1 trial; 18 participants; P = 0.26). Similarly, low-quality evidence from two trials indicates that behavioral interventions may have little to no impact on quality of life (standardized mean difference [SMD] –0.99, 95% CI –2.83 to 0.86; 55 participants). Specialized Professional Input A single trial of moderate quality suggested that structured assessment and management by continence nurse practitioners likely had little to no effect on the number of individuals achieving continence three months after treatment (risk ratio [RR] 1.28, 95% CI 0.81 to 2.02; 121 participants). This corresponds to an increase from 354 to 453 per 1000 individuals (95% CI 287 to 715). Complementary Therapies Five trials evaluated complementary therapies, including traditional acupuncture, electroacupuncture, and ginger-salt-partitioned moxibustion combined with routine acupuncture. Low-quality evidence suggests that these therapies may increase the likelihood of achieving continence after treatment. Participants receiving complementary therapy were approximately three times more likely to be continent (RR 2.82, 95% CI 1.57 to 5.07; 524 participants). This equates to an increase from 193 to 544 per 1000 individuals (95% CI 303 to 978). Adverse events, such as bruising and abdominal pain, were reported in one study involving electroacupuncture. Physical Therapy Two trials (three comparisons) suggest that transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) may reduce the average number of incontinent episodes in 24 hours (MD –4.76, 95% CI –8.10 to –1.41; 142 participants; low-quality evidence). One trial of TENS (two comparisons) indicated that the intervention likely improves overall functional ability (MD 8.97, 95% CI 1.27 to 16.68; 81 participants; moderate-quality evidence). Physical Therapy vs. Placebo One trial of transcutaneous posterior tibial nerve stimulation (TPTNS) found little to no difference in the number of participants achieving continence after treatment (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.19 to 3.04; 54 participants) or in the number of incontinent episodes (MD –1.10, 95% CI –3.99 to 1.79; 39 participants). At 26 weeks, one trial suggested improvement in the TPTNS group (odds ratio [OR] 0.04, 95% CI 0.004 to 0.41). However, no significant differences were observed in perceived bladder condition at six weeks (OR 2.33, 95% CI 0.63 to 8.65) or 12 weeks (OR 1.22, 95% CI 0.29 to 5.17). Quality of life, as measured by the ICIQ-LUTSqol, showed no significant difference (MD 3.90, 95% CI –4.25 to 12.05; 30 participants). Minor adverse events, such as skin irritation and ankle cramping, were reported. Pharmacotherapy One study evaluating estrogen therapy found no significant effect on the mean number of incontinent episodes per week in cases of mild incontinence (MD –1.71, 95% CI –3.51 to 0.09) or severe incontinence (MD –6.40, 95% CI –9.47 to –3.33). No adverse events were reported. Behavioral vs. Pharmacotherapy Interventions A single trial comparing a behavioral intervention (timed voiding) to a pharmacotherapy intervention (oxybutynin) did not provide usable data. Complementary Therapy Comparisons One trial compared different acupuncture techniques, finding that elongated needles resulted in a higher proportion of participants achieving continence (78.1%) compared to filiform needles (40%) after four courses of treatment (57 participants). However, the trial was assessed as having unclear or high risk of bias. Combined vs. Single Interventions A trial comparing a combined intervention (sensory motor biofeedback plus timed prompted voiding) to a single intervention (timed voiding) found that the combined approach may have little to no effect on the number of participants achieving continence (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.06 to 5.21; 23 participants) or the number of incontinent episodes (MD 2.20, 95% CI 0.12 to 4.28; 23 participants). Physical Therapy vs. Attention Control One study found that TPTNS may have little to no effect on the number of participants achieving continence compared to an attention control group performing stretching exercises (RR 1.33, 95% CI 0.38 to 4.72; 24 participants). This corresponds to an increase from 250 to 333 per 1000 individuals (95% CI 95 to 1000). Authors' Conclusions There is insufficient evidence to provide clear guidance on the management of urinary incontinence in adults during the rehabilitative phase after a stroke. The limited number of trials, small sample sizes, and wide confidence intervals make it challenging to determine clinically significant effects. Only four trials adequately concealed allocation, and many studies were poorly reported, raising concerns about potential bias. Larger, multicenter trials with robust methodologies are needed to establish effective interventions for post-stroke urinary incontinence.
